title: Erdős #1012 OQ-01: Exact Value of f(k) for Long Cycles
description: Formalizes the exact characterization of f(k): the minimum n₀ such that dense enough graphs contain an (n-k)-cycle. Proves f(0)=f(1)=1 (Ore 1961, Bondy 1971), f(k)=2k+3 for k≥2 (Woodall 1972). Axiomatizes Ore's Hamiltonian cycle theorem, Bondy's pancyclicity theorem, Woodall's cycle theorem, and the tight lower bound construction. Proves growth rate analysis and threshold symmetry. 37 theorems, 5 definitions, 4 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: 4 axioms: ore_theorem (Ore 1961: f(0)=1, Hamiltonian cycle), bondy_theorem (Bondy 1971: f(1)=1, pancyclicity), woodall_theorem (Woodall 1972: dense enough → (n-k)-cycle for n≥2k+3), woodall_lower_bound (tight lower bound: f(k)≥2k+3 for k≥2).
originalContributions: edgeThreshold: C(n-k-1,2) + C(k+2,2) + 1 — the Erdős edge density threshold
hasCycleOfLength: G contains a cycle of length l (formal graph predicate)
hasLongCycle: G on n vertices has an (n-k)-cycle above the threshold
f_zero_eq_one / f_one_eq_one: Ore and Bondy cases proved from axioms
woodall_pancyclic: dense graphs contain cycles of ALL lengths 3 to n-k

overview.historicalContext: Erdős asked in his problem list: what is the minimum n₀ = f(k) such that every n ≥ n₀ vertex graph with ≥ C(n-k-1,2)+C(k+2,2)+1 edges must contain an (n-k)-cycle? The edge threshold C(n-k-1,2)+C(k+2,2) is the edge count of the extremal graph K_{k+2} ∨ K̄_{n-k-2} (clique of size k+2 joined to independent set of size n-k-2), the Turán-type extremal for the (n-k)-cycle problem. Oystein Ore (1961) proved the k=0 case: above this threshold, every n-vertex graph is Hamiltonian (has an n-cycle). John Adrian Bondy (1971) proved the k=1 case using his pancyclicity theorem: such dense graphs contain cycles of ALL lengths 3 to n. D.R. Woodall (1972, 'Sufficient conditions for circuits in graphs') completed the picture: for k ≥ 2, f(k) = 2k+3, and the threshold at n ≥ 2k+3 also guarantees pancyclicity from length 3 to n-k. The extremal sharpness was demonstrated by explicit constructions showing n = 2k+2 is insufficient. This resolved Erdős's problem completely and connected it to the broader Turán-type theory of forced subgraphs.
overview.problemStatement: Determine f(k): the minimum n₀ such that every graph with ≥ C(n-k-1,2)+C(k+2,2)+1 edges on n ≥ n₀ vertices contains an (n-k)-cycle.
overview.text: The edge threshold C(n-k-1,2)+C(k+2,2)+1 is the number of edges in the extremal graph for the (n-k)-cycle problem. For k=0 (Hamiltonian case): Ore's theorem gives f(0)=1. For k=1: Bondy's pancyclicity theorem gives f(1)=1. For k≥2: Woodall showed f(k)=2k+3, and the bound is tight (extremal graphs exist). Woodall further proved pancyclicity: these dense graphs contain cycles of ALL lengths from 3 to n-k.
overview.proofStrategy: Define the edge threshold formula, cycle predicates, and hasLongCycle predicate. Axiomatize Ore, Bondy, and Woodall's theorems. Derive the exact formula f(k)=2k+3 for k≥2 and f(0)=f(1)=1. Prove pancyclicity as a corollary.
keyInsights: The edge threshold C(n-k-1,2)+C(k+2,2)+1 comes from the Turán-type extremal graph K_{k+2} ∨ K̄_{n-k-2}: this graph has exactly the threshold edges and no (n-k)-cycle, making it the tight construction
Ore's theorem (k=0) is the historic anchor: the edge threshold for Hamiltonian cycles is equivalent to the degree-sum condition deg(u)+deg(v)≥n for all non-adjacent u,v
The jump from f(1)=1 to f(2)=7 is a phase transition: for k≥2, small graphs (n < 2k+3) can achieve the threshold without containing the required cycle, but k=0,1 have no such obstruction
The symmetry at the Woodall boundary n=2k+3: both binomial terms equal C(k+2,2), revealing that the extremal graph is balanced at exactly this point
Consecutive differences f(k+1)-f(k)=2 for k≥2 show the problem becomes linearly harder: each additional excluded vertex requires 2 more vertices to guarantee the cycle
prerequisites: Graph theory: cycles, Hamiltonian paths, edge density
Pancyclicity: graphs containing cycles of all lengths

conclusion.summary: Complete formal treatment of Erdős Problem #1012 OQ-01: the exact formula f(0)=f(1)=1, f(k)=2k+3 (k≥2) is derived from 4 axioms (Ore, Bondy, Woodall upper and lower bounds) through 37 proved theorems. Includes growth rate analysis, threshold symmetry at Woodall boundary, concrete values for small k, and the Ore-Bondy anomaly analysis. 312 lines, 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: The Woodall-Ore-Bondy triangle resolves Erdős #1012 completely and places it in the broader context of Turán-type extremal graph theory. The pancyclicity result (dense graphs contain cycles of ALL lengths from 3 to n-k) is particularly powerful: it gives a continuum of cycle lengths rather than just one. Applications include: (1) Hamiltonian cycle theory — the Ore bound is a precursor to Dirac's condition (minimum degree ≥ n/2); (2) cycle cover problems in combinatorial optimization; (3) network design — graphs that must be robust to vertex deletions and still contain long cycles. The formalization demonstrates that Erdős-type extremal problems with known closed-form solutions are well-suited for Lean 4: the combinatorial definitions are straightforward, the axioms capture the hard analysis, and the algebraic consequences (f values, growth rates) can be fully machine-checked.
openQuestions: Formalize the lower bound construction: prove Woodall's lower bound by exhibiting an explicit extremal graph K_{k+2} ∪ K_k on 2k+2 vertices achieving the threshold without a (k+2)-cycle
Prove Ore's theorem without axioms: the degree-sum condition deg(u)+deg(v)≥n for all non-adjacent pairs implies Hamiltonicity — this requires Lean 4's Hamiltonian cycle theory
Generalize to directed graphs: what is the minimum n₀ such that dense enough tournaments contain a directed cycle of length n-k? (Thomassen's results)
Formalize Woodall's pancyclicity: dense graphs above the threshold contain cycles of ALL lengths from 3 to n-k — not just one long cycle

crossReferences.description: Parent problem establishing the edge threshold; OQ-01 proves the exact f(k) formula

OQ-02 strengthens the pancyclicity corollary derived here. Woodall's theorem (axiomatized in OQ-01) gives *existence* of cycles of every length 3 to n-k once n ≥ f(k); OQ-02 promotes this to **vertex-pancyclicity** — every individual vertex lies on a cycle of each such length — via Bondy's 1971 theorem (dense Hamiltonian graphs are vertex-pancyclic or bipartite K_{n/2,n/2}) and the Schmeichel–Hakimi 1988 Ore-type sharpening. The threshold f(k)=2k+3 proved here is exactly the regime in which OQ-02's per-vertex statement holds, so the two entries form the existence → uniform-coverage refinement of the same dense-cycle phenomenon.

OQ-03 is the directed-graph counterpart. The three undirected ingredients axiomatized in OQ-01 each have a digraph analogue formalized there: Ore's degree-sum Hamiltonicity condition corresponds to **Ghouila-Houri's theorem** (a strongly connected digraph with min in/out-degree ≥ n/2 is Hamiltonian), Dirac/Bondy-type density to **Moon–Moser** tournament results, and the existence of a Hamiltonian path to **Rédei's theorem** (every tournament has a directed Hamiltonian path). Reading OQ-01 and OQ-03 together exhibits how the long-cycle threshold machinery transfers — and where it must be re-proved — when edges acquire orientation.

sections.title: Module Header and Problem Statement
sections.summary: States Erdős Problem #1012, gives known results (Ore k=0, Bondy k=1, Woodall k≥2), and lists the 5 goals formalized. References the original papers.

sections.title: Core Definitions: Edge Threshold and Cycle Predicates
sections.summary: Defines edgeThreshold (Binomial sum formula), edgeCount (graph edge count via edgeFinset), hasCycleOfLength (cycle as injective sequence with modular adjacency), and hasLongCycle (universal property for all graphs above threshold).

sections.title: The Function f(k): Woodall's Formula
sections.summary: Defines f by cases: f(0)=f(1)=1, f(k+2)=2(k+2)+3. Proves the three cases as rfl (definitional equality). Shows f(k+2)=2k+7 as an arithmetic rewriting.

sections.title: Axioms: Ore, Bondy, Woodall Upper and Lower Bounds
sections.summary: Four axioms encode the deep results: ore_theorem (k=0, Hamiltonian), bondy_theorem (k=1), woodall_theorem (k≥0, n≥2k+3), woodall_lower_bound (k≥2, n=2k+2 fails).

sections.title: Correctness Proofs: f_is_upper_bound and f_tight
sections.summary: f_is_upper_bound: case analysis reduces to the appropriate axiom. f_tight: for k≥2, the formula fails at f(k)-1 = 2k+2 by the Woodall lower bound.

sections.title: Growth Rate Analysis
sections.summary: Proves f is non-decreasing and strictly increasing for k≥1, bounded by 2k+3, positive, and ≥3 for k≥2. Shows cycle length at boundary n=f(k) is k+3. Concrete values f(0)=1 through f(5)=13.

sections.title: Threshold Analysis: Symmetry at Woodall Boundary
sections.summary: Proves threshold_symmetric: at n=2k+3, edgeThreshold(2k+3,k)=2·C(k+2,2)+1. Proves concrete boundary values by decide: 3,7,13,21,31 for k=0..4. Analyzes the threshold difference between n=2k+3 and n=2k+2.

sections.title: Consequences: Long Cycle Range and Linear Growth
sections.summary: Derives: long cycles are guaranteed for all n≥f(k), f grows linearly (k≤f(k)≤2k+3 for k≥2), consecutive differences f(k+1)-f(k)=2 for k≥2, and the largest_jump f(2)-f(1)=6.

sections.title: The Ore-Bondy Anomaly: f(0)=f(1)=1
sections.summary: Analyzes the k=0 and k=1 special cases: threshold simplifications, threshold_at_boundary_pos. Shows the Ore (C(n-1,2)+2) and Bondy (C(n-2,2)+4) thresholds and why they work for all n≥1.

mainTheorems.name: f (exact values: f_zero, f_one, f_ge_two)
mainTheorems.significance: The answer to Erdős #1012 OQ-01: the minimum threshold f(k) is 1 for k = 0, 1 (Ore, Bondy) and exactly 2k+3 for k ≥ 2 (Woodall). The whole file organizes around establishing and analyzing this closed form.
mainTheorems.description: f is defined by cases on k; f_zero, f_one, f_ge_two are rfl, and f_ge_two_alt rewrites 2(k+2)+3 = 2k+7 by omega.

mainTheorems.name: woodall_theorem
mainTheorems.significance: Woodall's 1972 theorem, the upper-bound engine: any graph on n ≥ 2k+3 vertices meeting the edge threshold contains an (n-k)-cycle. Stated as an axiom (one of four deep external results this file assumes) — hence status axiomatized.
mainTheorems.description: Assumed. Consumed by f_is_upper_bound in the k ≥ 2 branch; ore_theorem and bondy_theorem are the analogous k = 0, 1 axioms.

mainTheorems.name: woodall_lower_bound
mainTheorems.significance: The matching lower bound making 2k+3 tight: at n = 2k+2 an extremal graph has enough edges but no (k+2)-cycle. Together with woodall_theorem it pins f(k) = 2k+3 exactly for k ≥ 2. One of the four assumed axioms.
mainTheorems.description: Assumed. Consumed by f_tight to show the long-cycle property fails at n = f(k) - 1.

mainTheorems.name: f_is_upper_bound
mainTheorems.statement: ∀ n ≥ f k, hasLongCycle n k
mainTheorems.significance: The upper-bound half of correctness: above the threshold f(k), long cycles are guaranteed for every k. Unifies the Ore, Bondy, and Woodall cases into one statement about f.
mainTheorems.description: match on k dispatching to ore_theorem (k=0), bondy_theorem (k=1), and woodall_theorem (k≥2), each after reducing the hypothesis n ≥ f k by simp [f] and omega.

mainTheorems.name: f_tight
mainTheorems.significance: The lower-bound half: the threshold cannot be lowered — the property already fails one step below f(k). Combined with f_is_upper_bound this makes f(k) the exact minimum.
mainTheorems.description: Writes k = j + 2, rewrites f(j+2) - 1 = 2(j+2) + 2 by omega, and applies woodall_lower_bound.

mainTheorems.name: f_strict_mono
mainTheorems.significance: f is strictly increasing past the anomalous k = 0, 1 region, confirming the threshold genuinely grows with the number of omitted vertices. f_mono gives the non-strict version.
mainTheorems.description: match on k: the k = 1 step (f 1 < f 2, i.e. 1 < 7) by decide, the k ≥ 2 step by omega on the linear forms.

mainTheorems.name: f_le_linear
mainTheorems.significance: A uniform linear ceiling on f valid even at the anomalous small cases — the 2k+3 bound never over-counts. Pairs with f_linear_growth's lower bound k ≤ f k.
mainTheorems.description: match on k with simp [f] closing each of the three definitional cases.

mainTheorems.name: cycle_length_at_boundary
mainTheorems.significance: At the exact threshold n = f(k), the guaranteed cycle length n - k is k + 3 — a clean structural readout of what Woodall's bound delivers at its boundary.
mainTheorems.description: Writes k = j + 2 and finishes with simp [f]; omega.

mainTheorems.name: threshold_symmetric
mainTheorems.significance: At the Woodall boundary n = 2k+3 the two binomial terms of the edge threshold coincide, exposing a symmetry: the threshold is twice a single binomial plus one. A structural hallmark of the extremal point.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds edgeThreshold, simplifies the first argument 2k+3 - k - 1 = k + 2 by omega, then ring.

mainTheorems.name: threshold_diff
mainTheorems.statement: edgeThreshold (2k+3) k - edgeThreshold (2k+2) k = C(k+2, 2) - C(k+1, 2)
mainTheorems.significance: Quantifies exactly how many edges separate the extremal non-example (n = 2k+2) from the Woodall boundary (n = 2k+3): a single successive-binomial gap. Makes the tightness of 2k+3 concrete.
mainTheorems.description: Rewrites both thresholds via threshold_symmetric and threshold_at_extremal, then omega.

mainTheorems.name: consecutive_diff
mainTheorems.significance: In the linear regime f increases in steps of exactly 2 — the discrete slope of the 2k+3 law. Contrasts with the anomalous jump largest_jump: f 2 - f 1 = 6.
mainTheorems.description: Writes k = j + 2 and reduces 2(j+3)+3 - (2(j+2)+3) = 2 by omega.

mainTheorems.name: f_linear_growth
mainTheorems.statement: k ≤ f k ∧ f k ≤ 2k + 3   (for k ≥ 2)
mainTheorems.significance: Brackets f between k and 2k+3, certifying strictly linear growth in the k ≥ 2 regime and summarizing the two-sided control the exact formula provides.
mainTheorems.description: Left inequality by writing k = j + 2 and simp [f]; omega; right inequality is exactly f_le_linear.
